title: Thermal Hydraulic Optimization of an Immersion Cooled Battery Module
role: ME 598: Electronics Cooling — Graduate Course Project
brief: Redesigned a 9-cell cylindrical EV battery module for immersion cooling in ANSYS Icepak, achieving a 46% reduction in peak cell temperature and cutting thermal variation from 23.7 °C to 7.0 °C while also reducing system pressure drop.
overview:
Thermal management is one of the primary challenges limiting battery performance, safety, and lifespan in electric vehicles. Elevated cell temperatures accelerate degradation, while temperature nonuniformity leads to uneven aging, capacity imbalance, and reduced pack reliability. This project investigated immersion cooling as an alternative to conventional battery cooling strategies for a 9 cell cylindrical battery module.

The objective was not only to reduce peak cell temperature, but also to improve temperature uniformity across the module while minimizing hydraulic losses. Using CFD driven design iterations in ANSYS Icepak, multiple coolant candidates, flow configurations, and cell arrangements were evaluated to identify a thermally efficient and hydraulically practical cooling solution.
contributions: Developed a detailed 3D battery module model in SolidWorks and implemented a thermal fluid simulation framework in ANSYS Icepak, including heat generation profiles, coolant properties, boundary conditions, and flow domains.
Evaluated six candidate coolants using a comparative thermal hydraulic assessment based on thermal conductivity, viscosity, pressure drop, and temperature uniformity characteristics.
Selected an ethylene glycol water mixture (EG 50 50) through a systematic tradeoff analysis balancing thermal performance and pumping requirements.

Redesigned coolant flow paths and battery cell arrangement to improve coolant distribution throughout the module, targeting simultaneous reduction of peak temperature and inter cell thermal gradients.
Validated the redesigned configuration through CFD simulations, quantifying the impact of geometric modifications on thermal performance, flow behavior, and hydraulic resistance.
outcomes: Achieved a 46 percent reduction in peak cell temperature compared with the baseline configuration.
Reduced temperature variation across the battery module from 23.7 °C to 7.0 °C, representing approximately 70 percent improvement in thermal uniformity.
Reduced system pressure drop while simultaneously improving cooling effectiveness, demonstrating an improved thermal hydraulic balance rather than a single metric optimization.
Established a comparative performance framework for coolant selection and thermal management design evaluation in immersion cooled battery systems.
challenges: Peak temperature reduction and temperature uniformity are often competing objectives. Flow configurations that effectively cool localized hot spots can create uneven coolant distribution and larger temperature gradients across the module. Achieving improvements in both metrics required iterative refinement of flow paths and cell placement.

Many cooling enhancements improve heat transfer at the expense of increased pumping power. Understanding which geometric changes contributed to thermal improvement versus hydraulic penalty was critical to developing a balanced design.

Comparing multiple coolant candidates required evaluating coupled thermal and flow effects rather than relying solely on thermal conductivity, since viscosity and flow resistance significantly influence overall cooling system performance.
